title: Yitro: the first word (Exodus 20:2)
hookLine: the Ten Words begin not with a rule but with "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out"
tomorrow: Yitro: the last word is inside (Exodus 20:14)

lines: A JOB STARTS WITH A HANDBOOK.
cards: A new job usually starts with a handbook: hours, dress code, what gets you fired. A marriage doesn't start that way. Nobody opens a wedding with a list of house rules.
It starts with names, and a story: who we are to each other, what we've already been through. The mountain is wrapped in smoke. Thunder, lightning, the sound of a horn growing louder.
The people tremble at the foot of Sinai. Then the voice speaks the first of the Ten Words. It sounds like the moment for a rule.

teach.h: I AM THE LORD THY GOD.
teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." No command in it. No thou shalt.
Just I, and you, and what happened between us.
The very first Hebrew word is anochi, I.

There's a shorter everyday word for I, ani; anochi is the fuller, weightier one, and the Talmud, playing with its letters, reads them as the initials of a short Aramaic phrase: I myself wrote it and gave it.
In Jewish tradition this whole verse counts as the first of the Ten Words. That's the Torah's own name for them, aseret ha-devarim, the ten words or ten statements, not ten commandments.
Traditions number the ten in different ways, and that's fine; this is how Jewish tradition counts.

The medieval poet and philosopher Judah Halevi asked: why doesn't God introduce himself as the one who created heaven and earth? Wouldn't that be grander? His answer: the people at the mountain hadn't seen creation.
They had seen Egypt. They had walked out. So God speaks through what they themselves lived: not the God of the philosophers, but the God of your own story.
Everything after this, every rule about Shabbat and parents and honesty, rests on that first sentence.
First a relationship. Then the rules.

how: The Ten Words are read in synagogue in the portion Yitro, in Va'etchanan in Deuteronomy, and on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah; in some congregations people stand while they are chanted.

o: the Lord: a title used in place of God's name
commandment: a rule given at Mount Sinai
I: the fuller, weightier Hebrew word for I

games.q: inside the first word — tap the pairs.

s: the first of the Ten Words begins with thou shalt
it begins with I: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out.
the Torah calls them the ten words, not the ten commandments
aseret ha-devarim: ten words, or ten statements.
Judah Halevi asked why God didn't mention creating the world here
his answer: the people had seen Egypt, not creation.

games.q: you're about to speak to a trembling people at Sinai for the first time. how does the first word begin?
o: with who I am, and what I did for you.
games.why: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt. the relationship comes first.

practice: Remember one thing that once held you and doesn't anymore: a fear, a job, a habit, a diagnosis that turned out all right. Let yourself recall the day you knew you were out, and who or what brought you out.
If you pray, you can say the verse's own opening, I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out, and hear it spoken to you; if not, stay with the memory of the open door.

wordCard.voice: Anochi. I. The first word God speaks at Sinai: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out. A relationship before a rule.

orig.note: Hebrew: I. the first word of the Ten Words, a fuller form than the everyday ani.

carryVoice: Your line: first, a relationship. It begins with I, and you, and a story. Until tomorrow.
